title: Shortest Word Distance II
description: Brute force to optimized: re-scanning the whole array on every query versus precomputing per-word index lists once and merging them per query.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Design a class initialized with an array of words, wordsDict, that supports repeated shortest(word1, word2) calls, each returning the shortest distance between any occurrence of word1 and any occurrence of word2 in wordsDict. word1 and word2 may be different for each call.

blocks.text: Given a fixed array of words, answer many queries, each asking for the shortest distance between any occurrence of one word and any occurrence of another.

blocks.title: Analogy: Repeatedly Finding the Closest Pair of Two Kinds of Landmarks on a Fixed Map
blocks.text: Picture a fixed map with landmarks of many different types, and repeatedly being asked, for two DIFFERENT types each time, how close together their nearest instances are. Since the map itself never changes, it pays to organize landmark positions by type once, rather than re-scanning the whole map for every question.

blocks.caption: Precompute every word's occurrence list once; reuse it for every query

blocks.text: shortest("coding","practice") is 3 (indices 3 and 0); shortest("makes","coding") is 1 (indices 1 or 4, and 3, closest pair distance 1).
Before re-scanning the entire array for every query, notice that precomputing each word's list of occurrence indices, just once, lets every later query work directly from those lists.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since the same wordsDict is queried repeatedly, scanning it fresh for every shortest() call repeats the same work across many queries.

Observation 2: Precomputing a map from each word to its sorted list of occurrence indices, once, up front, gives instant access to any word's positions for every later query.

Observation 3: Given two sorted lists of positions (for word1 and word2), the shortest distance between any pair can be found with a two-pointer merge, always advancing whichever pointer points to the smaller position, in O(occurrences) instead of checking every pair.

Observation 4: This turns each query into work proportional only to how often the two specific words appear, not the size of the whole array.
This leads to precomputing an index map once at construction time, then answering each shortest() query with a two-pointer merge over the two words' index lists.
On every shortest() call, scan the entire array directly, tracking the most recent position of each word and updating the best distance whenever the other word is seen.

items: For every shortest(word1, word2) call, scan wordsDict from the beginning.
Track the most recent index of word1 and word2 seen so far.
Whenever either word is seen, if the other has also been seen, update the best distance.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every query re-scans the entire wordsDict array from the beginning, regardless of which two words are being asked about.
This repeats essentially the same scanning work, over and over, across every one of up to 5000 queries.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) per shortest() call, where n is the array length; O(q times n) across q queries.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the stored array.

Limitation: re-scanning the entire array for every query is wasteful, since the array never changes; precomputing occurrence positions once would let each query work only with the relevant words' positions.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why re-scanning every query is wasteful: the array is fixed once constructed, so the position of every word can be precomputed a single time and reused for every future query.

What to precompute: a map from each distinct word to its sorted list of occurrence indices, built once during construction.

How to answer a query efficiently: given the two words' sorted index lists, a two-pointer merge finds the closest pair of positions in time proportional to how often each word occurs, not the whole array's length.

The core idea: precompute an index map once; answer each shortest() query with a two-pointer merge over the two relevant index lists.

During construction, build a map from each word to its sorted list of occurrence indices in wordsDict. On shortest(word1, word2), retrieve both words' index lists and merge them with two pointers: repeatedly compare the current positions, update the best distance, and advance whichever pointer holds the smaller position.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: precomputed index lists, two-pointer merge per query

blocks.text: Since each word's index list is already sorted (built by scanning left to right once), a two-pointer merge correctly finds the closest pair of positions across the two lists: advancing the pointer at the smaller position always moves toward a potentially closer pair, without ever needing to check every combination of the two words' occurrences.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) once, at construction, to build the index map; O(occurrences of word1 plus occurrences of word2) per shortest() call.
Space: O(n) for the index map.

blocks.text: Shortest Word Distance II is a direct lesson in amortizing repeated-query costs: precompute once at construction, and let every later query work only with the relevant precomputed data, here via a two-pointer merge over sorted occurrence lists.

items: Re-scanning the array on every query instead of precomputing occurrence indices once.
Using a nested loop over both index lists (checking every pair) instead of a linear two-pointer merge.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "this will be called many times", think: precompute per-word index lists once, and merge them per query instead of rescanning.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs each shortest() call in O(n) time. The optimized approach spends O(n) once at construction, then O(occurrences) per call. Both use O(n) space.

items: Pattern: precompute per-word occurrence indices once; answer each query with a two-pointer merge.

Core Idea: build a map from word to sorted occurrence indices at construction; for each query, merge the two relevant index lists to find the closest pair in linear time relative to their occurrences.
Time: O(n) per call for the brute force, O(n) once plus O(occurrences) per call for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized index map.
Most Important Observation: since the same array is queried repeatedly, precomputing once at construction amortizes the cost across every future query.
Interview Difficulty: a standard "precompute once, query fast" design problem.
One line memory trick: precompute index lists once, two-pointer merge per query.
